questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman presented with left arm pain and swelling for several hours. She was an active intravenous drug user. On examination, there was minimal erythema in the left antecubital fossa and upper arm with significant pain on palpation. Investigations: CT left arm: gas seen in fascial planes, suspicious for a necrotizing soft tissue infection
questions.lead_in: In addition to emergency surgical debridement, what would be the most appropriate antibiotic regimen?
questions.explanation: Piperacillin–tazobactam, vancomycin, clindamycin Necrotizing soft tissue infection calls for empiric antibiotic coverage of Gram-positive (including methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, MRSA), gram-negative, and anaerobic bacteria. Clindamycin is added to inhibit toxin production. Piperacillin–tazobactam, vancomycin, clindamycin provides the most appropriate coverage, including that of MRSA.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q25

questions.question: A patient with acute myeloid leukemia presents with fever, hypotension, and swelling of the right thigh, with discolouration, bullae formation, and crepitus. An aspirate is performed and a Gram stain is shown. [image-based question: Gram stain of muscle aspirate]
questions.question_raw: A patient with acute myeloid leukemia presents with fever, hypotension, and swelling of the right thigh, with discolouration, bullae formation, and crepitus. Aspirate is performed. Presented with a gram stain.

parts.text: What type of organism is shown in the Gram stain?
What is the most likely organism?

parts_raw.text: What type of organism is shown in the gram stain?
What is the most likely organism?

questions.model_answer: a) Large gram-positive bacilli (rods) with blunt ends and few accompanying polymorphonuclear leukocytes; subterminal spores may be seen. b) Clostridium septicum — the cause of spontaneous (nontraumatic) gas gangrene, which arises by the bacteremic route in neutropenic hosts with hematologic malignancy and gastrointestinal mucosal lesions. (In traumatic gas gangrene C. perfringens predominates, but this spontaneous presentation in AML points to C. septicum, and the subterminal spores on Gram stain support it.)

questions.question: Gas gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis).

parts.text: One clinical and one Gram stain characteristic suggestive of infection?

parts_raw.text: One clinical and gram stain characteristic suggestive of infection?

questions.model_answer: a) Clostridium perfringens (80%–95% of cases, most common); C. novyi (10%–40%) and C. septicum (5%–20%, the usual cause of spontaneous nontraumatic disease). b) Clinical: severe pain out of proportion to findings with crepitus/tissue gas and bronze skin discolouration with serosanguineous foul-smelling discharge. Gram stain: many large gram-positive bacilli with blunt ends and few/no polymorphonuclear leukocytes. c) Principal mediator is the C. perfringens alpha-toxin; principal setting is penetrating muscle injury contaminated with soil/foreign material and devitalized tissue (e.g., compound fracture, war or surgical wounds, arterial insufficiency). d) (1) Prompt, extensive emergency surgical exploration with excision/debridement of involved muscle, fasciotomy, and amputation if required. (2) High-dose penicillin G (up to 24 million units/day IV) combined with clindamycin 600 mg IV q6–8h. e) Alpha-toxin (a lecithinase/phospholipase C) causing myonecrosis, hemolysis, intravascular thrombosis and myocardial suppression/hypotension; the theta-toxin (perfringolysin O) is the other major virulence factor.

cohort_answer.text: C. perfringens (most common), C. septicum, C. sordellii, C. novyi. Clinical: gas in subcutaneous tissue, pain out of proportion, SIRS, dish water fluid. Gram stain: large GPB (boxcar shaped = C. perfringens; terminal spores/drumstick = C. septicum), minimal PMNs due to lethal alpha toxin. Settings: trauma injury (C. perfringens), colon adenocarcinoma/neutropenia (C. septicum); accidental traumatic injuries, war wounds, surgical wounds (bowel/biliary/septic abortion), arterial insufficiency. Management: urgent surgical debridement; empiric PipTazo/Vanco/clinda, once Clostridium confirmed Pen 24mU/day IV + Clindamycin 600mg IV q6h. Virulence factor: Alpha toxin (lecithinase damaging cell membranes, causes hemolytic anemia/thrombosis/myonecrosis/hypotension); Theta toxin (perfringolysin O) decreases microvascular perfusion and causes DIC

questions.question: A woman has a history of intermittent bloody diarrhea for the last month. She presents with hypotension and new hemorrhagic bullae on her lower extremities. A Gram stain of a sample shows Gram-positive rods with subterminal spores and no other cells visible. [image-based question: Gram stain of Gram-positive rods with subterminal spores, no other cells visible]
questions.question_raw: A woman has a history of intermittent bloody diarrhea for the last month. She comes in with hypotension and new hemorrhagic bullae to her lower extremities. A sample is taken, with the gram stain appearing as follows (photo of Gram Positive rods with subterminal spores, no other cells visible on stain):

parts.text: What are two characteristic features on Gram stain?
What is one risk factor for this condition?
What is the recommended antimicrobial treatment?
What are two other interventions you might consider?

parts_raw.text: a) What are two characteristics features on Gram stain?
c) What is one risk factor for this condition?
d) What is the recommended antimicrobial treatment?
e) What are two other interventions you might consider?

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Gram-positive bacilli (rods). (2) Subterminal (or terminal) spores, with a paucity of accompanying inflammatory cells on the stain.
b) Clostridium septicum.
c) Underlying colorectal (or other GI) adenocarcinoma; other risks include hematologic malignancy/neutropenia, cyclic or congenital neutropenia, diabetes, and prior bowel ischemia. The month of bloody diarrhea points to a colonic portal of entry, classically occult colon cancer.
d) High-dose penicillin G (3-4 million units IV q4h) PLUS clindamycin (600-900 mg IV q8h) for antitoxin/protein-synthesis-inhibitory effect. Carbapenem (meropenem/imipenem) is an alternative beta-lactam.
e) (1) Urgent surgical debridement/exploration of involved tissue (source control is essential in clostridial myonecrosis/spontaneous gas gangrene). (2) Aggressive hemodynamic resuscitation and ICU support; hyperbaric oxygen may be considered as an adjunct, and given the association, workup for underlying colon cancer.
questions.beyond_mandell: Penicillin-clindamycin combination and surgical debridement for spontaneous gas gangrene follow standard IDSA SSTI guidance (Stevens et al., IDSA 2014).

cohort_answer.text: Gram stain: Gram positive bacilli, subterminal spores. Organism: Clostridium septicum (if no trauma; C. perfringens if trauma). Risk factor: spontaneous gas gangrene with diarrhea history suggests GI entry, possible undiagnosed adenocarcinoma of colon; also congenital neutropenia or prior radiation to abdomen. Treatment: Penicillin 3-4 million U IV q4h + Clindamycin 600-900mg IV q8h (alternatives imipenem, meropenem or vancomycin). Other interventions: debridement/surgical intervention, hyperbaric oxygen as adjuvant.
